What is the difference between Self-Attention and Cross-Attention ?

These are two types of attention mechanisms that fall under soft attention and are very important concepts to under stand LLMs.

So, What are they and what are the differences between them ?

The names give a hint:

Self-attention

In this type of attention tokens from the same sequence attend to each other, meaning they find relationships among themselves.

Data types: In this case, the data types between which the relationships are calculated are the same.


Masking: One important thing to note in self-attention, particularly when used in LLMs for next word/token prediction, is the risk of data leakage. If we allow the current token to attend to future tokens, it can lead to data leakage.

To avoid this, the attention between the current and future tokens is set to zero, a process known as masking.




Cross-attention

There tokens from different sequences attend to each other, i.e., they find relationships between sequences.

Data types: The data types of the sequences used are different. For example, one sequence could be in English and the other in German, or in a task like speech-to-text.

No Masking: In cross-attention, there is no need for masking because the sequences represent different types of data streams.


In summary:

Self-attention involves the same sequence (same data types) and requires masking.

Cross-attention involves different sequences (different data types) and doesn’t require masking.

After months of working on AI for automated video editing, Dikshant and I have decided to wrap up Compass AI. While we considered this possibility when we started, it still feels uneasy to accept that we didn’t make it.

That said, we made good progress and explored multiple approaches. Two of them were promising but not scalable for the creative demands of video editing:

1/ LLM-based Decision Making – using large language models to pick effects from a set list, but videos started to look the same after a certain point.

2/ Code Generation for Effects – generating code for custom effects from examples. This approach showed promise, but the examples didn’t perform as well as expected. We would have doubled down on this direction if we’d had enough resources (server).

We also considered diffusion-based approaches, but due to resource limitations, we weren’t able to pursue them.

Captions recently launched an auto-editing feature, but it’s based on templates. This forces the video content to fit the template, which doesn’t feel natural, and videos created this way tend to look similar.

We thought about pivoting to something more achievable with the resources we had, but couldn’t find a natural pivot. We wanted to push the boundaries of LLMs and do something truly novel.

On the customer front, we received an unexpected number of inquiries to use the product. The challenge wasn’t with market interest, but with the product itself.

I’m grateful for everything we learned along the way, and for the people we met. It was a new role for both of us. Special thanks to Sachin Udas dai and Atulya Acharya dai for everything you did for us. Huge thanks to everyone who tested and supported us throughout this journey.

I’ll continue working at the intersection of Software Engineering and LLMs.

If you’d like to know more about our journey or hear specific details, feel free to reach out.

My biggest takeaway thus far from TEDAI Vienna ?

The importance of creating frameworks that can improve AI outputs.


It’s not actually the focus of the event mainly, but…I think it’s a bit of a spot we’re not paying attention to…enough.

What we feed LLMs (like ChatGPT) dictates the output, obviously. But we’re not great, as humans, to come up with generative frameworks to feed INTO generative AI.

The better we get at building new types of flexible frameworks/pedagogies, the better our machine learning will get.

When you feed generative AI generative, flexible frameworks (like the recipe-free cooking method we teach at RecipeKick) they create customized, surprising results.

When you feed it rote, step by steps…it spits that back out.

🧑‍⚖️ Revolutionizing Evaluation with LLMs(LLM AS A JUDGE)! 🌟

Evaluating outputs from Large Language Models (LLMs) can be complex due to varied quality criteria like relevance, coherence, and clarity. Enter LLM-as-a-judge! By leveraging LLMs for scoring, we automate evaluations while ensuring a human-like understanding of context.

Key steps in implementing LLMs as judges include:
Creating Clear Prompts: Provide detailed task descriptions and scoring scales to guide LLMs effectively.
Using Human Baselines: Establish a dataset with human evaluations for reliable comparison and to reduce noise in scores.
Iterative Improvements: Continuously refine prompts to enhance accuracy, including utilizing few-shot examples and structured outputs.

With these strategies, we've achieved impressive correlations between LLM ratings and human assessments.
